canonical_concept.beeja: ॐ (Om) — the primordial offering. Also स्वाहा (Svāhā) — the mantra of offering in fire rituals.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Yajña is a masculine noun derived from the root yaj (to worship/sacrifice) with the suffix -na. The root yaj is one of the most important roots in Vedic Sanskrit — it gives yajña (sacrifice), yajus (sacrificial formula), yajamāna (sacrificer), and Yajurveda (the Veda of sacrificial formulas).
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Yajña is the foundational principle of Vedic civilization — the sacred act of offering that maintains cosmic order (ṛta). The Bhagavad Gītā (3.10-16) describes yajña as the cosmic cycle: Brahmā created beings along with yajña; through yajña, rain falls; from rain, food grows; from food, beings live; beings perform yajña — the wheel of cosmic reciprocity. Yajña operates at five levels: Brahma-yajña (study of Vedas), Deva-yajña (fire offerings to gods), Pitṛ-yajña (offerings to ancestors), Bhūta-yajña (offerings to all beings), Manuṣya-yajña (hospitality to humans).
canonical_concept.dhatu: यज् (Yaj) — To worship, to sacrifice, to offer.
canonical_concept.nirukta: Yāska: "yajyate devā anena iti yajñaḥ" — that by which the gods are worshipped. Yajña is the act of offering that creates and maintains the relationship between humans and the divine.
canonical_concept.tattva: Yajña-Tattva — the principle of sacred exchange and cosmic reciprocity. The universe itself is a yajña — a continuous cycle of giving and receiving between all levels of existence.

claims.value: In Mīmāṃsā: yajña is the primary means of achieving all human goals — dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. The apūrva (unseen potency) of yajña persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita: yajña at the highest level is the offering of the ego into the fire of knowledge (jñāna-yajña). In the Bhagavad Gītā: karma-yoga is yajña — all action performed without attachment is an offering to the divine.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: In Vedic cosmology: the universe itself was created through a cosmic yajña — the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90) describes the primordial sacrifice of the cosmic Puruṣa from which all creation emerged. The concept of yajña as the mechanism of cosmic maintenance — the gods depend on yajña for their sustenance.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: Yajña as psychological principle: the offering of the ego (ahaṃkāra) into the fire of self-knowledge is the highest yajña. The Bhagavad Gītā (4.24-33) describes multiple forms of yajña as psychological practices: offering the senses into the fire of restraint, offering actions into the fire of knowledge.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: Rāja-sūya (royal consecration) and Aśvamedha (horse sacrifice) are the primary royal yajñas. The king's yajña maintains the prosperity of the kingdom. The concept of rāṣṭra-yajña (national sacrifice) — governance as a form of yajña for the welfare of all.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: In Āyurveda: yajña smoke (dhūpa) is used for purification and healing. The concept of yajña as environmental medicine — fire offerings purify the atmosphere. Modern research on yajña smoke (homa therapy) suggests antimicrobial properties.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: The Śulbasūtras (altar-building manuals) contain the earliest known mathematical theorems, developed for constructing yajña altars of precise areas. The Pythagorean theorem, geometric transformations, and irrational numbers appear in the context of yajña altar construction.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: The timing of yajñas is determined by Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy). The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) for yajña is based on astronomical calculations. The Nakṣatra system was developed partly for determining the correct times for yajña.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: The sacred fire (agni) of yajña is the basis of all metallurgical fire. The concept of dhātu-yajña (offering of metals) — specific metals are offered in specific yajñas for specific results.

provenance.source_text: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)

claims.value: The five mahāyajñas (great sacrifices): Brahma-yajña, Deva-yajña, Pitṛ-yajña, Bhūta-yajña, Manuṣya-yajña. The Soma yajña (Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Rājasūya) are the major Vedic sacrifices. The agnihotra (daily fire offering) is the minimal yajña obligation.

claims.value: The fire symbolizes yajña — the transformative medium of offering. The smoke rising from the fire symbolizes the offering reaching the divine realm. The svāhā (offering mantra) symbolizes the act of giving without reservation.
